video_title: Why Coldcard's 5-Year-Old Bug Let Hackers Take Over $100M in Bitcoin: Uneasy Money
gist: Kane Warwick, security researcher Taylor Monahan and guests dissect a 2021-vintage entropy bug in Coldcard hardware wallets that is letting brute-force crackers (explicitly not North Korea) drain 1,600+ BTC across at least four attacker 'waves', then move to the trade.xyz SKHEX perp oracle blow-up and the venue's duty to block insane trades, and finally to the fight over EIP 8361's proposed ETH issuance cut. The through-line is mechanism design: fallbacks, oracles and monetary-policy knobs all produce tail consequences worse than the problem they were meant to fix.

themes.theme: Coldcard entropy bug: scale and mechanics

insights.claim: Coldcard hardware wallets shipped a broken entropy (randomness) routine in 2021 that sat in the codebase unnoticed for five years, meaning every seed phrase generated in that window is potentially crackable.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Any BTC held on a Coldcard seed generated 2021-2026 should be treated as compromised and swept to a freshly generated wallet on different hardware.
insights.quote: They screwed it up in 2021. It that in the in the codebase it was used for 5 years before someone just discovered it.

insights.claim: Losses from the Coldcard bug are already over $100 million and roughly 1,600 BTC across thousands of addresses and probably thousands of victims, per Galaxy Research's ongoing victim-report and on-chain clustering work.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Sizing the loss as nine figures in BTC makes this one of the largest self-custody failures on record and a live supply overhang as attackers liquidate.
insights.quote: Thousands and thousands of addresses, probably thousands of victims.

insights.claim: Because cracking weak-entropy keys requires throwing large amounts of compute at each key, the Coldcard drains will keep arriving in waves for weeks and months rather than in a single event.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Expect a rolling drip of stolen-BTC flows and victim headlines; a one-week-old story is not a closed story for exchange compliance or for sentiment.
insights.quote: we are going to see losses for the coming weeks and even months, right?

insights.claim: On-chain analysis has identified at least four distinct 'waves' of attacker activity against Coldcard seeds, which may represent up to four separate threat actors rather than one.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Multiple independent crackers means no single takedown stops the bleed and no single mixing/laundering pattern to trace.

insights.claim: Coldcard's marketing decision to retain no customer data — positioned as the anti-Ledger stance after Ledger's data leak — left the company with no channel to warn affected users to move funds.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Zero-data privacy postures carry an unpriced incident-response cost; buyers of hardware wallets should weigh notification capability against data minimalism.
insights.quote: We're not Ledger. We don't keep any data.

insights.claim: Weak-entropy key cracking follows the same exponential cost curve as vanity-address generation: a few characters are cheap to brute force, but each additional character multiplies the compute required.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: A usable mental model for judging whether any given key-generation shortcut is safe: only the exponent matters, and small reductions in randomness collapse security entirely.

insights.claim: Monahan argues entropy bugs are the worst class of wallet vulnerability because losses are non-custodial, unrecoverable, and play out over an extended period with no way to patch already-generated keys.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Rank entropy/key-generation risk above smart-contract risk when underwriting wallet vendors or custody providers.
insights.quote: entropy issues and wallets are the worst vulnerability. like the absolute worst

themes.theme: Attribution: brute-force crackers, not North Korea

insights.claim: The Coldcard thefts are not North Korean: DPRK crews specialize almost exclusively in social engineering, which already earns them billions, and do not run the multi-decade compute-heavy cracking operations this attack requires.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Default 'it's Lazarus' attribution is wrong here; the actor set is professional password/database crackers with GPU farms, implying different laundering behavior and no sanctions-driven freeze path.
insights.quote: North Korea, they do social engineering. That's it. They're very good at it. It makes them billions of dollars.

insights.claim: The likely profile is that the first wave was a lone researcher who found the bug (possibly with AI assistance), while later waves are established professional cracking outfits that already brute-force passwords and databases at scale and simply retuned their scripts for compute profitability.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Any protocol or wallet with historic weak randomness should assume a standing, economically rational cracking industry will find it the moment the payoff clears compute cost.
insights.quote: it's just a matter of turning the knobs on how much compute right to make sure that they're profitable

insights.claim: Claims that AI found the Coldcard bug 'in two minutes' are contaminated: once an exploit is public, models retrieve public write-ups rather than independently rediscovering the flaw.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Discount post-hoc AI vulnerability-discovery demos; only sandboxed, tool-stripped tests on pre-disclosure code bases are evidence for the AI-finds-bugs thesis.
insights.quote: there's a big post on Reddit right now that said Claude can find it in two minutes. It's It's actually not finding it in two minutes. It's It's finding other Reddit posts

themes.theme: Codebase red flags investors and users can actually check

insights.claim: The Coldcard flaw was hard to spot because randomness generation hopped across repositories and languages — Python plus C or Go — forcing a reviewer to traverse a chain of libraries to see where the fallback occurred.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Cross-repo, cross-language dependency chains are where security review breaks down; treat them as a due-diligence red flag in any custody stack.
insights.quote: God, this codebase was a mess, guys. Go look at your code bases that you're relying on.

insights.claim: Cryptographic code should fail loudly rather than fall back — the Matthew Green rule from the 2015 TrueCrypt audit is that code unable to obtain confident randomness 'should barf and catch fire'.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: A concrete audit test for any wallet or key-management vendor: does the RNG path have any silent fallback? If yes, that is the vulnerability.
insights.quote: If your code cannot get the randomness necessary or initialize the process like with any amount of confidence, then it should barf and catch fire.

insights.claim: Normal product engineering rewards graceful fallbacks and punishes error messages as bad UX, and that instinct is exactly inverted for cryptography — which is how a silent fallback to a weak library survived five years.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Explains the recurring pattern behind entropy bugs and predicts more of them as general-purpose engineering norms bleed into crypto primitives.
insights.quote: but with cryptography you do not want that you want it to be dead simple

insights.claim: AI coding agents amplify the fallback anti-pattern — the host bans fallbacks as rule number three in all of his repos because agents, and Codex especially, will stack five layers of them and hide the real failure.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Expect a rising incidence of silently-degraded security code in AI-assisted repos; explicit no-fallback rules are a cheap mitigation worth demanding from portfolio teams.
insights.quote: one of the things that I have in all of my repos like it's like number three is no fallbacks right um because they will make a chain of fallbacks that

insights.claim: Coldcard never had a single security audit, so Monahan's realistic advice to users is to ask vendors for their audits and actually read them rather than to read firmware.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: An unaudited custody vendor holding billions is a screenable red flag; audit existence is verifiable without technical skill.
insights.quote: ask your teams about their audits right these guys didn't have a single security audit and then actually read those audits,

insights.claim: Non-technical users can assess wallet vendor risk from process signals — one person committing directly to main with no peer review or build process is a strong negative signal, whereas Ledger and Trezor run large, organized teams with commit, review and build discipline.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: A repeatable, non-technical diligence checklist for custody vendors: team size, commit hygiene, peer review, build system, audits.
insights.quote: if it's one person committing directly to Maine and without any peer review, without any process, usually a very bad sign.

insights.claim: The Coldcard team allegedly antagonized security researchers and well-known Bitcoin developers who tried to understand the codebase, which suppressed the outside review that would normally surface such a bug.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Hostility to researchers is a leading indicator of undiscovered vulnerabilities and belongs in vendor risk scoring.

insights.claim: Monahan is not broadly worried that hardware wallets are the next attack vector — she frames Coldcard as a perfect storm of complex code, tiny dev team and no audits, and maintains that opsec failures, phishing and social engineering remain the larger expected-loss channel for users.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Argues against a sector-wide de-rating of hardware wallet vendors; the idiosyncratic risk sits with small, unaudited teams.
insights.quote: This specific one is just scary because you can't it's very hard for like it's very hard to give end users any advice and that's why it is painful.

insights.claim: The failure was partly a community failure — hardcore Bitcoiners extended trust to Coldcard on ideological alignment rather than verifying engineering process.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Ideological trust substitutes for diligence across crypto; the same dynamic is a repeatable source of loss in other maximalist-aligned products.

themes.theme: Dice entropy and the limits of user-supplied security

insights.claim: Coldcard's dice-rolling feature, marketed as extra offchain entropy, was itself the source of earlier losses: almost all the pre-2026 Coldcard victims Monahan has seen were dice rollers who did not roll enough times.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Security features that offload work to users can invert into the primary attack surface; the 'trust nothing, roll your own entropy' ethos produced weaker keys, not stronger.
insights.quote: In almost all cases, those people were the dice rollers.

insights.claim: Scattered Coldcard victim reports exist for every year from 2021 through 2025 on Reddit and on chain, meaning the bug was being quietly exploited long before the current free-for-all.
insights.speaker: Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Isolated, unexplained self-custody losses are a leading indicator of a systemic key-generation flaw and deserve aggregation rather than dismissal.

insights.claim: Guidance that only works if users perform 50 dice rolls is a design failure because real users quit after three to ten rolls, so security has to be made easy rather than delegated to discipline.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host) and Taylor Monahan
insights.so_what: Products whose safety depends on tedious user compliance should be underwritten at the compliance rate observed in practice, not the instructions.
insights.quote: I'm just saying if you tell an American to roll that dice 50 times, they're not rolling.

themes.theme: trade.xyz oracle blow-up and venue responsibility

insights.claim: A SKHEX perp on trade.xyz printed a real thin pre-market trade that dropped the mark from about $1,128 to $917 before recovering almost immediately, liquidating a wave of users on a price that lasted seconds.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Concrete demonstration that RWA perps inherit pre-market and closed-market pricing gaps that crypto-native assets do not have; a recurring liquidation-hunting vector.

insights.claim: trade.xyz made users whole but declared it a one-time non-precedent, which is itself a strong opinionated claim about what the 'real' price of an asset is — a judgment DeFi venues are supposedly not meant to make.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Watch for venues quietly adopting NASDAQ-style trade-busting discretion; it changes the risk profile and the regulatory surface of 'permissionless' perp venues.
insights.quote: the challenge for for DeFi is like you're not even supposed to be involved in this right like it's supposed to be contracts and stuff and all of a sudden you're like making post hawk judgments about what the real price was

insights.claim: Warwick's core oracle framework is that there is no such thing as the price of an asset — price is a construct, so a venue must instead write an explicit rule set for which prints count.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Evaluate perp and lending protocols on the explicitness of their price rule set, not on which oracle brand they use.
insights.quote: there is no such thing as the price of an asset, right? It is like a a some kind of a construct.

insights.claim: Mike from Ether.fi argues front-end operators have an ethical duty to hard-block wildly insane trades — not warn, block — the way Interactive Brokers stops retail from self-destruction, and says Uniswap and trade.xyz should do the same.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in DeFi front-ends toward brokerage-style paternalism; determined users get pushed to raw contracts, which changes where flow and liability sit.
insights.quote: somebody tries to do a trade with 70% price impact or some crazy slippage. You probably should just shouldn't let the user do that. Forget warnings and red text. Like you shouldn't let them do that.

insights.claim: Ether.fi hit the same problem in beta — users lost money on trades the team believes it should not have permitted — and is rebuilding trading with those guardrails over the coming weeks.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: A near-term product change at a major LRT issuer; guardrails becoming table stakes raises the bar for smaller front-ends.

insights.claim: Warwick attributes the industry's reflexive 'we have no responsibility' posture to regulatory fear from the Gensler era rather than to genuine conviction about permissionlessness.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: As that enforcement threat recedes, expect front-ends to add intervention features they previously avoided — a real change in DeFi product design.

insights.claim: The guest describes stakehouse's 'metaoracle' on Morpho, which combines fair market value with primary redemption value and flags when the two deviate enough to switch between them, as a prudent template for lending-protocol asset pricing.
insights.speaker: guest, 3F Labs co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete, deployed design for LST/LRT and stablecoin pricing that avoids both hardcoded $1 pegs and raw market whiplash.

insights.claim: Every oracle safeguard shifts risk into the tail: a switch designed to protect against the two-sigma case can kill everyone in the three-sigma case, and the disaster you engineer against usually is not the one that arrives.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: A general heuristic for underwriting protocol upgrades: ask what the safeguard does in the tail, not in the base case.
insights.quote: often times the thing that you're trying to prevent ends up not actually being the real thing. It's some other thing that you didn't think about

insights.claim: The ETH staking exit-queue fear proved to be the wrong worry — the entry queue turned out to be the binding constraint, an example of mechanism designers guarding the wrong direction.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that staking-flow panic narratives are often directionally inverted; useful when pricing ETH unstaking-driven supply scares.

themes.theme: EIP 8361 and the ETH issuance cut fight

insights.claim: EIP 8361, which would cut ETH issuance, was posted with only a 48-hour comment window ahead of consideration for the upcoming hard fork, with no consultation of major Ethereum protocol builders.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: Process risk is now a live variable for ETH holders: a monetary-policy change to a ~$500bn network could be railroaded on a two-day notice.
insights.quote: there's the CIP that's been proposed with a 48 hours to provide comments before it basically goes into you know consideration or vote

insights.claim: Blended ETH staking yield is currently around 2.5% including MEV, and Mike argues cutting issuance would drive it toward roughly 20 basis points.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: The magnitude of the proposed cut — 2.5% to ~0.2% — is the key number for modelling staking-ratio and LST economics under EIP 8361.
insights.quote: because suddenly your yield goes down to you know 20 basis points which is probably you know where it'll end up

insights.claim: Cutting issuance would be bearish for ETH price on its own logic, because collapsing yield would push tens of billions of dollars of currently staked ETH back into circulating float where it can be sold.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: If EIP 8361 gains traction, the trade is unstaking-driven float expansion, not the deflationary bid its proponents advertise.
insights.quote: so now you're going to have tens of billions of dollars of ETH unstaked and you know out there in the in the market

insights.claim: Mike's stated view is that while he would not personally argue for it, the case for raising ETH issuance is stronger than the case for cutting it — and the strongest option is leaving it alone entirely.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: A prominent LRT operator publicly framing the issuance debate as asymmetric in the opposite direction to the proposal is a meaningful governance signal.
insights.quote: the argument to increase issuance is in my mind actually stronger than the argument to to decrease it

insights.claim: An issuance cut would kill ETH looping overnight, hitting Lido, ether LSTs and lending protocols where ETH-looping activity makes up a large share of dapp revenue.
insights.speaker: guest, 3F Labs co-founder
insights.so_what: The direct equity-like exposure to EIP 8361 sits in LST issuers and ETH lending markets; their revenue lines are the transmission channel.
insights.quote: ETH looping would be you know killed overnight and ETHOP in many cases uh you know make up a big part of the um the DAP revenues

insights.claim: The guest, who worked on this issue at stakehouse since the 2024 minimum-viable-issuance debate, says Ethereum's process compares badly to the FOMC's structured signalling and that the proposal arrived with no consultation despite two years of published input.
insights.speaker: guest, 3F Labs co-founder
insights.so_what: Monetary-policy governance quality is itself a valuation input for ETH; institutional allocators benchmark against central-bank-style process.
insights.quote: this is worse than like um at least FOMC has like a right structure and uh process and um signaling uh that makes a whole system much more reliable

insights.claim: The guest argues the same deflationary effect can be achieved through fee burn from growth rather than an austerity cut, citing a 2024 Rebbit Capital thesis that put Ethereum's 'owner earnings' north of $7 billion — roughly 3% of ETH market cap.
insights.speaker: guest, 3F Labs co-founder
insights.so_what: Reframes the issuance debate as growth versus austerity and gives a specific yardstick (owner earnings / market cap) for valuing the network.
insights.quote: owner earnings was like north of 7 billion

insights.claim: The guest argues tradfi marginal buyers want yield, a revenue growth story and buybacks — all of which favour a growth strategy over an issuance cut that risks Ethereum's security budget and centralises staking by rugging solo stakers.
insights.speaker: guest, 3F Labs co-founder
insights.so_what: Identifies which ETH narrative actually converts institutional flows, and why an austerity narrative may repel the buyer it needs.

insights.claim: Warwick argues zero money-supply growth is not defensible economics in any school — calling it 'a Bitcoin brainworm' — since money supply should expand with the growth of the economy or you get deflation.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the ultrasound-money framing that underpins ETH supply-cut advocacy and, by extension, part of the ETH bull thesis marketing.
insights.quote: there's not a lot of economists out there hard hardly any that would argue that a 0% increase in the money supply per year is a good idea.

insights.claim: Warwick notes the ultrasound-money narrative was an accident of EIP-1559, which Vitalik designed to stabilise a wildly oscillating fee market for UX reasons, not to create a burn story.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Cautionary precedent that protocol changes generate narratives their designers never intended — relevant to how any issuance change would be marketed and mispriced.
insights.quote: let's not forget 1559 was not supposed to be about ultrasound money it was a really good idea to make the fee market more stable in Vitalik's idea

insights.claim: Mike argues most cryptoeconomic networks would kill for a higher staking ratio and that the proposal appears driven partly by an ideological dislike of liquid staking tokens, with the likely outcome being more centralisation rather than less.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi)
insights.so_what: If the anti-LST motive is real, LST issuers face recurring governance attacks independent of the economics — a persistent policy risk to price into that sector.
insights.quote: most cryptoeconomic networks would kill to have more people stake their token like they view that as a positive

insights.claim: Warwick argues a significant majority of ETH stakers are not financially motivated, citing his own validators earning roughly 0.5% after downtime and slashing without changing his behaviour, so yield cuts may move less stake than models assume.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Cuts against both bull and bear ETH unstaking models; the marginal staker, not the average one, is what matters for float.
insights.quote: I don't think that your marginal ETH staker is sitting there going the the yield is is like the primary driver, right?

insights.claim: Warwick identifies the issuance push as an efficiency argument inherited from EF thinking — that Ethereum should stake the absolute minimum ETH needed for security — and argues it ignores real-world incentives.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Naming the underlying philosophy explains why the proposal will recur regardless of this vote's outcome.
insights.quote: Ethereum should have the absolute minimum amount of ETH staked that is required to secure the network.

insights.claim: Mike expects EIP 8361 to keep returning even if it fails now, because a committed constituency will keep pushing it; Warwick separately thinks it is very unlikely to pass in this round.
insights.speaker: Mike (Ether.fi) and Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Treat issuance-cut risk as a standing, recurring overhang on LST and ETH-yield business models rather than a single binary event.

insights.claim: Warwick frames EIP 8361 as the 'be careful what you wish for' consequence of decentralising the Ethereum Foundation: researchers who left to form independent, mandate-narrow orgs are now free to push single-issue proposals nobody can veto.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Structural change in how Ethereum protocol risk arrives — expect more frequent, more aggressive proposals from small orgs, raising governance variance for ETH.
insights.quote: I would file this in like the be careful what you wish for.

insights.claim: Warwick's hot take is that more chaos and less monoculture in Ethereum governance is net positive, because the fight broke a multi-year governance apathy in which outsiders felt they had no chance against EF-set narratives.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: A bullish read on governance conflict as engagement rather than dysfunction — useful counterweight when headlines frame Ethereum infighting as decay.
insights.quote: more chaos in Ethereum and and less kind of uh you know this um monoculture um is probably good

insights.claim: Warwick's general rule for protocol changes is that touching a working mechanism invites unforeseen reflexive consequences, so with a full menu of Ethereum problems — privacy, interop, 12-second block times, gas costs — monetary policy is the wrong knob to turn.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: A prioritisation lens for judging which Ethereum roadmap items actually move adoption versus which are ideological.
insights.quote: if you touch something, be prepared for it to touch you back

insights.claim: The guest invokes the Buffett/Munger 'better to be roughly right than precisely wrong' principle against fine-tuning issuance, arguing there is no correct issuance level and knob-turning risks being precisely wrong plus an endless sequence of corrective upgrades.
insights.speaker: guest, 3F Labs co-founder
insights.so_what: Gives allocators a defensible frame for opposing parameter activism in monetary policy of any crypto network.
insights.quote: it's, you know, better to be roughly right than precisely wrong

insights.so_what: x

themes.theme: Protocol strategy shifts: Aave retrenchment, Lido consolidation

insights.claim: Aave is retreating from its aggressive multi-chain 'be everywhere' expansion, having concluded that deploying to every L2 and obscure L1 is negative EV given the risks assumed on those chains.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: If the leading lending protocol judges long-tail chain deployment negative EV, long-tail chains lose their anchor DeFi liquidity — bearish for new-chain TVL narratives.
insights.quote: this is negative EV to be everywhere there's a bunch of like risks that we're taking by being on these chains

insights.claim: Lido is about to consolidate its validator set so operators no longer need one validator per 32 ETH, materially lowering the operational cost of staking.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: Lower staking friction pushes the staking ratio up just as EIP 8361 tries to push it down — the two forces collide on ETH float.
insights.quote: Lido is about to like collapse all their validators to like five valid you know making it easier to not have to run one validator for every 32E

insights.claim: A Kobe post declaring that trade.xyz is not raising money coincided with the SKHEX oracle incident, which Warwick reads as a reliable tell that something chaotic is happening behind the scenes.
insights.speaker: Kane Warwick (host)
insights.so_what: A social-signal heuristic: unprompted denials from well-connected figures often front-run disclosed problems at the named venue.
